content: Good morning. I want to walk you through where we stand on the staffing side, because a lot has moved in the last week or two. The menu is locked — Marco and I signed off on the final version three days ago, and we had a small dinner at his apartment to mark the occasion, which felt like the right way to close that chapter — so the pressure has fully shifted now to making sure we have the right people in place before we open. I've been doing interviews and reference checks pretty intensively over the past few weeks, sometimes two or three per day, and I think we're close to a complete picture for the launch team. I've also had Tanabe-san review the salary figures against what he's seeing in the broader Tokyo independent restaurant market, which has been useful as a sanity check. Let me go through the hires one by one, starting with the kitchen, because that's where I wanted to be most deliberate and where I felt the stakes were highest.

Good morning, Kenta. It's genuinely good to hear the menu is finalized — that's a significant weight off, and it means every conversation about staffing can now be tied to concrete roles and specific responsibilities rather than moving targets. The menu being locked also means that whoever you bring into the kitchen knows exactly what they're being asked to execute from day one, which I think is an underappreciated advantage during an opening period. Please go ahead and walk me through the kitchen first. I'll take notes as you go and I'll probably have questions about how each person fits into the overall team structure once you've given me the full picture, particularly around how responsibilities will be distributed during the nights when the full team isn't present. What does the kitchen lineup look like?

So the most important hire on the kitchen side is the sous chef. Marco and I talked for a long time about the profile we needed — someone who could run the line on the nights Marco isn't physically in the kitchen, someone who genuinely understands northern Italian technique rather than just being a competent general cook who can follow a recipe sheet. We interviewed five candidates over about three weeks. The person we landed on is Haruki Nakajima. He is 29 years old, which I know sounds young for a sous chef role at an opening like this, but when you sit across from him and talk about food for an hour and then watch him work, the age stops mattering very quickly. He came to us from Trattoria Goccia — that's a serious Italian kitchen in Shibuya that's been putting out consistent work for about eight years. He was there for four years, the last two of which he spent as a junior sous chef. Before Goccia he did a stage in Bologna for six months, which is actually part of why Marco responded to him so strongly. They share a reference point for the way Emilian kitchens think about pasta. His knife work is exceptional, his sauces are clean without being overcomplicated, and honestly, his mise en place discipline is the kind of thing that will set the tone for everyone else in that kitchen.

Haruki Nakajima sounds like a genuinely strong fit given what Marco is trying to build. The Trattoria Goccia background is meaningful — Shibuya Italian kitchens that have sustained eight years are usually running a disciplined operation, so if he came up through that environment as a junior sous chef, he's not just someone who can cook, he's someone who has learned how to maintain standards under volume and pressure. The Bologna stage is also a real differentiator. Shared culinary vocabulary between a head chef and sous chef matters enormously, especially in the early months when you're still establishing rhythms. What's the compensation structure you've worked out with him? And I'm curious about the conversation around what his actual scope of authority will be on the nights Marco steps back.

On compensation, we agreed to 380,000 yen monthly salary. I'll be honest — he was probably worth asking for more, and I think he knows that. But he was also transparent with me that he wanted the opening experience specifically, and that he's thinking of this as a two-to-three-year chapter where he builds something from the ground floor rather than inheriting an established kitchen. So the number reflects a mutual understanding that the opportunity itself is part of the package. Tanabe-san reviewed the figure against market data and said it's within the reasonable range for his experience level in Tokyo, leaning toward the lower end, which is why I want to make sure we revisit this at the six-month mark if things are going well. On the scope question — Marco was actually very deliberate about this in our conversations with Haruki. On the three nights a week when Marco won't be in service, Haruki has full authority on the pass. He can call changes to plating if the product coming out of the kitchen isn't meeting the standard. He can manage kitchen staff scheduling in real time. He cannot change menu items or pricing without Marco's sign-off, which is documented in the job description. I think that's a healthy boundary for an opening period.

The 380,000 yen structure makes sense in the context you're describing. An opening sous chef role at a serious independent concept in Higashi-Azabu isn't an anonymous line position — he's getting equity in the story of the place, a restaurant name on his CV that can mean a great deal if Osteria Morishita builds the reputation Marco is aiming for. I think the framing you've both landed on, where the opportunity is part of the compensation package, is honest and sustainable as long as the six-month review is treated as a genuine commitment and not a placeholder. To that point: I'd recommend including the review date explicitly in the employment contract rather than leaving it as a verbal understanding between you. Goodwill is high at the offer stage, but written terms protect both parties when circumstances get complicated later. The scope delineation also sounds well thought through. Full pass authority is real authority — it means he owns the quality of what goes out the door on those nights, and kitchen staff will read very quickly whether he has genuine standing or is just nominally in charge — but anchoring menu changes to Marco protects the concept's identity during the period when the kitchen culture is still forming. How does Haruki feel about reporting to Marco given that Marco is Italian and they'll be navigating some degree of cross-cultural working dynamic? Did that topic come up during the interview process?

It came up, and I appreciated that Haruki raised it himself rather than us having to bring it into the room. He said — and I'm roughly paraphrasing — that he's spent enough time around Italian kitchen culture both in Japan and in Bologna that he's not walking in with illusions about how direct Marco can be when something isn't right. He actually said that's part of what he's looking for, because he's been in Japanese kitchens where nobody says anything negative until it's too late to fix it, and he finds that more exhausting than a chef who just tells you exactly what's wrong in the moment. Marco met him twice before we made the offer, and the second meeting went significantly longer than I expected. I had to text Marco afterward to ask if everything was okay, and he said they'd spent forty minutes talking about a specific preparation of a ragù from a trattoria in Modena they'd both eaten at different times, completely by coincidence. So I think the dynamic is going to be fine. Now, do you want me to move to the front of house, or do you have more questions on the kitchen side?

That story about the Modena ragù is actually a good sign — shared culinary obsession is one of those things you can't manufacture in an interview process, and when it surfaces spontaneously it usually means the working relationship will have genuine depth rather than just professional courtesy. The fact that they found a common reference point independently, at different times and without coordinating in advance, suggests their culinary instincts are genuinely aligned at a fairly specific level, not just in broad direction. That kind of alignment tends to make conflict resolution easier because there's a shared aesthetic standard to return to when disagreements arise. I'm satisfied with the kitchen picture for now — I have a clear sense of Haruki as a hire and how he fits relative to Marco. Please go ahead and walk me through the front of house. I know service tone is going to be one of the most defining characteristics of how Osteria Morishita is experienced by guests, and it's also the area where an independent opening can most easily get the culture wrong in ways that are slow to correct. I'm curious about how you've thought through that hire.

The front of house conversation has actually been one of the most interesting parts of this whole process for me, because it forced me to be very precise about what kind of service experience I want guests to have. This isn't a white-tablecloth formal dining room, but it's also not a neighborhood trattoria where the waiter shouts the specials from across the room. I kept coming back to the word 'ease' when I was thinking about it — I want guests to feel completely at ease, never made to feel like they're performing, never made to feel like they're missing a code. That's actually much harder to train for than technical service skills, so I was looking for someone senior enough to build and hold that culture rather than just execute individual service moments well. The person I've brought in as service manager is Eiko Sawada. She is 41 years old, and she has one of the most interesting service backgrounds I've encountered in the Tokyo restaurant space. She spent seven years managing the dining room at a Michelin two-star kaiseki restaurant in Kyoto before she moved back to Tokyo four years ago. Since then she's worked at two western-concept fine dining restaurants in Minato-ku. She's never been in an Italian kitchen specifically, but when I talked to her about the service philosophy I was describing — that idea of 'ease' — she immediately gave it back to me in more precise language than I had. She called it 'invisible competence,' which is exactly what I meant. You only notice the service when something goes wrong. When it's working, you just feel comfortable. I thought that was exactly right.

Eiko Sawada is a compelling hire, and the kaiseki background is not an obvious choice for an Italian concept — but I think you're right that it may actually be an advantage. Kaiseki service at a Michelin two-star level requires a form of spatial awareness and guest-reading that is genuinely transferable, and it's a discipline where 'invisible competence' isn't just a philosophy, it's a survival requirement. Guests who have spent serious money on a kaiseki meal have a very well-tuned sense for when service attention is slightly off, and a dining room manager who has thrived in that environment for seven years has had her instincts calibrated by some of the most demanding guests in Japan. The Minato-ku western fine dining experience also means she's not walking into a foreign register — she's already made that transition once. What is her compensation, and how do you plan to structure her relationship with the part-time floor staff? I imagine the onboarding challenge is partly about translating her very high service standards into a team that may have significantly less experience.

Her salary is 460,000 yen per month. She pushed back a little on the initial number I offered, which was 440,000 yen, and I think she was right to. Her Minato-ku references were excellent, and when I spoke to her most recent employer — I asked for permission first and she gave it without any hesitation, which itself told me something — they were genuinely enthusiastic about her. One of them said, and I'm quoting more or less exactly, 'the dining room ran better on the nights Sawada-san was managing than on the nights I was there myself.' That kind of feedback is not something I was willing to walk away from over 20,000 yen a month. On the floor staff question — this is something Eiko and I spent about an hour discussing in our second meeting, and I was impressed by how clearly she had thought it through already, even before she knew for certain she had the position. She wants to run a proper pre-service briefing every single shift, not just on the busy nights. She said the mistake a lot of independent restaurants make is treating pre-service as optional when it's quiet, and then the team doesn't have the habit built in when it actually matters. She's also proposed something she called a 'shadow system' for the first month of service, where the more experienced full-time staff are paired with the part-time staff on every shift, not just to supervise, but to demonstrate by example. I like that approach. It's not punitive, it's mentorship-structured. Now let me tell you about the part-time staff, because I think those choices are also interesting.

The 460,000 yen figure is justified, and the way you got there — through a reference call that turned into a genuine endorsement rather than a pro forma confirmation — is exactly the kind of diligence that protects an opening. The pre-service briefing discipline Eiko is proposing is also a meaningful indicator of how she thinks about service culture. A team that briefs every night, regardless of cover count, is a team that treats service as a craft rather than a task. The shadow system for the first month is smart structurally because it embeds the standard into muscle memory before pressure arrives, not during it. Who are the part-time staff, and how did you find them?

We have two part-time servers joining us for the opening. The first is Yui Tachibana, who is a university student — she's in her third year studying hospitality management at Rikkyo. She came to us through a recommendation from the program coordinator at Rikkyo, who apparently has an informal relationship with a few independent restaurants in the area and reaches out when she has students looking for serious placements rather than just casual part-time work. What made Yui stand out in the interview was that she came prepared. She had looked at our location, thought about the concept, and had a set of genuine questions rather than just answering mine. She's also studying Italian on her own, which I found charming and also potentially useful as the language of the menu and the wine list is something guests sometimes have questions about. She can commit to three evenings a week plus weekend lunch service, which is very workable. The second part-time hire is Naoki Hirose. Naoki is different from Yui in that he's not a student — he has a full-time job in a completely unrelated field, IT project management, and he does restaurant service specifically because he loves it. He's been doing part-time floor work at various Shibuya restaurants for about six years, so his technical service skills are significantly stronger than most part-timers I would expect at his availability level. He can do two evenings a week reliably. I was a little uncertain initially about whether someone with a full-time day job would have the mental energy to bring to the floor after a full day of work, but his references from previous restaurants were uniformly strong, and one of the managers I spoke to said he was the most focused part-time staff member they'd had in years. So I decided that track record matters more than the theoretical concern.

Yui Tachibana and Naoki Hirose are well-matched choices for very different reasons, and the fact that they fill different scheduling windows is a practical advantage for the rota. Yui brings energy, genuine curiosity, and three evenings plus weekend lunch, which is significant coverage for someone still in university. The self-study Italian is a minor detail that could end up being a real service moment — a guest who is surprised that a server can explain a wine name or a preparation term in the original language tends to remember that interaction. Naoki's six years of accumulated floor experience across multiple Shibuya restaurants essentially means Eiko doesn't have to start his training from zero, which reduces the load on the shadow system she's designing. The concern about dual-role fatigue is real, but your instinct to weight the actual track record over the theoretical risk is correct — if his previous managers say focus is consistent, that's a pattern, not luck. So let me make sure I have the full roster clear in my head. Can you give me the complete opening staff count, full-time and part-time combined, so I can see the whole team at once?

Yes — so as of right now, the total opening team is 5 full-time, 2 part-time. Full-time is Marco Petrelli as head chef, Haruki Nakajima as sous chef, Eiko Sawada as service manager, and then two additional full-time kitchen staff who I haven't gone into detail on today but who are essentially confirmed — one is a pasta specialist who worked under Marco's recommendation from a contact he brought from his network, and the other is a commis chef who's just finished culinary school but who Marco auditioned in a working session and was impressed enough with that he flagged her as someone worth bringing in from day one rather than waiting to see how she develops. Part-time is Yui Tachibana and Naoki Hirose, as I described. So yes — 5 full-time, 2 part-time. Seven people total going into opening. I feel genuinely good about this group. There's range here — Eiko's experience depth at the top, Yui's freshness and curiosity at the other end, and everyone in between chosen with some real deliberateness. I just want to make sure the onboarding period holds it all together before service starts.

That's a well-structured team for a 64.5 square meter space — you have genuine depth in the leadership tier with Marco, Haruki, and Eiko, and you've made thoughtful choices at every level below that. Seven people with this combination of backgrounds, if the onboarding period is handled well, should be able to establish a service identity before you open rather than discovering it piece by piece through early guest feedback. What I find particularly coherent about this roster is that the range is intentional. You've described every hire in terms of what specific function they fill and why their background suits it, rather than assembling a group of generically capable people and hoping they find their own level. That intentionality tends to translate directly into team cohesion during the high-stress pre-opening period. On that subject: what does the onboarding timeline look like? Do you have a confirmed start date for the full team to come together, and do you have a sense of how many days of internal rehearsal service you want before the first actual guests are in the room? I ask because with a team that spans from Michelin two-star dining room management to third-year university student, the calibration work during those rehearsal sessions will carry a disproportionate amount of the load that formal training documentation alone can't fully accomplish.

The plan right now is to have everyone confirmed and contracts signed by the end of September, which I think is achievable. October is the full onboarding month. I'm targeting a soft opening — invited guests only, no public bookings — in the first week of November. The thinking is that the full team comes together in the kitchen and dining room starting October sixth, and we run internal rehearsals through roughly mid-October. That gives us about ten days of proper rehearsal service with real food and real plating before we move into the soft opening phase. I've also asked Eiko to design a service briefing document — something that captures the philosophy in writing rather than just in verbal instruction — so that as we bring in future part-time staff beyond Yui and Naoki, the foundational tone is documented and doesn't depend entirely on Eiko being in the room. Marco is doing something similar on the kitchen side, which I believe is partly for his own clarity and partly because Haruki asked for it. Haruki apparently told Marco that he works better when the chef's standards are written down rather than implied, which I thought was an admirable piece of self-knowledge for someone his age. That kind of communication about one's own working style is exactly what you want from someone stepping into a sous chef role at an opening. I feel like the team has a healthy self-awareness about what it needs to function well. That's the best sign I can point to as we head into this next phase.

The October onboarding timeline with a soft opening in early November is realistic and gives the team a reasonable runway without dragging out the pre-opening period so long that momentum starts to feel abstract. Ten days of rehearsal service is meaningful if the rehearsals are run with full discipline — real timing, real plating standards, real service sequences — rather than treated as casual run-throughs. Eiko's service briefing document is an excellent initiative, and it signals something important about how she thinks about institutional continuity rather than just personal performance. The parallel move from Haruki — asking for Marco's standards in writing — tells you something similar. Both of them are thinking about how the kitchen and dining room function as systems, not just as collections of talented individuals. That is exactly the organizational instinct you want from people in those roles at an opening. You've put together a thoughtful team, Kenta. The compensation decisions are defensible, the scope definitions are clear, and the onboarding structure has real logic to it. The main thing I would flag as a watch item going into October is making sure the rehearsal period genuinely stress-tests the handoff moments — specifically the pass between Haruki and Eiko's floor team on the nights Marco isn't in service. Those transitions are where opening-period misunderstandings tend to accumulate. If you build in deliberate scenarios that force those communication channels to be tested under mild pressure before guests arrive, you'll be in a strong position for the soft opening.
